q: How do decisions, judgments and reasoning relate, and what is inductive reasoning?
a: A decision is the process of choosing between alternatives, and reasoning is the process of drawing conclusions. Decisions are based on the judgments people make, and inductive reasoning is one of the primary mechanisms involved in making judgments. Inductive reasoning means reasoning from observations to conclusions that are probably, but not definitely, true. It is the basis of scientific investigation, where observations are made, data are collected and conclusions are drawn. The strength of an inductive argument depends on the representativeness, number and quality of the observations. Many white swans support an expectation about swan color, but one clearly observed black swan contradicts the claim that every swan is white, so a single high-quality observation can carry substantial weight. In everyday life, people use past experience to predict what will happen, especially in familiar situations, and some of this induction happens automatically.

q: What is a heuristic, and how do the availability and representativeness heuristics differ?
a: Heuristics are rapid rules of thumb that use past experience to guide present behavior. They are likely to give a correct answer but are not foolproof, because they reduce the amount of information a person considers by relying on a readily available cue, which usually fits the situation but can point away from the correct judgment. The availability heuristic judges by how readily examples come to mind, and the representativeness heuristic judges by how much a case resembles a category. The difference is which property supplies the shortcut, accessibility in memory or similarity to a familiar kind of case.

The availability heuristic makes events that are more easily remembered seem more probable. The more examples a person can think of, the more probable the event seems. That is useful when memorable events are frequent, but memorability is also affected by distinctiveness, emotional salience and frequent encoding or retrieval, none of which make an event more common.

q: How do the r-words and causes-of-death judgments show the availability heuristic?
a: In the word judgment, about 70 percent of respondents say English has more words beginning with r than words with r as the third letter, but words with r third are actually three times more common. Retrieving words by first letter is easier, so those words feel more numerous. For causes of death, asthma is more likely than botulism or a tornado, yet many pick the less likely cause. A death from botulism can become front-page news while deaths from asthma go virtually unnoticed, so distinctive coverage makes the unusual cause easier to bring to mind.
note: The three-to-one figure is not verified. The commonly stated ratio is closer to two to one. The direction, that words with r are more common in third position, holds.

q: What is the representativeness heuristic and base-rate neglect, and how do the Robert and lawyer–engineer problems show it?
a: The representativeness heuristic bases a judgment on how much one event resembles another, so a person decides whether A belongs to class B from how well A’s properties match what is normally associated with B. Base-rate neglect is when that similarity displaces the background prevalence of the categories. Robert wears glasses, speaks quietly and reads a lot, and many people say he is more likely a librarian than a farmer. But America has about 2.2 million farms and 120,000 libraries, so the base rate favors farmer. In the lawyer–engineer problem a group has 70 lawyers and 30 engineers. With no other information, the chance of an engineer is 30 out of 100 and people use that correctly. When Jack is described as conservative, careful, ambitious and enjoying home carpentry, sailing and mathematical puzzles, people tend to call him an engineer. So base rates are used when they are all that is available and disregarded once descriptive information is given.
note: The 2.2 million and 120,000 are counts of farms and libraries, not of people in each occupation. Farmers still outnumber librarians, so the conclusion stands, but the comparison is loose.

q: What is the conjunction rule, and why is the Linda problem an error?
a: The conjunction rule states that the probability of two events occurring together cannot be greater than the probability of either event alone, since every case satisfying both conditions also satisfies each one. Linda is described as single, outspoken, bright, trained in philosophy, concerned with discrimination and social justice, and involved in antinuclear demonstrations. About 82 percent choose Linda is a bank teller and active in the feminist movement over Linda is a bank teller. The extra detail makes the description fit the person they were told about, but feminist bank tellers are a subset of bank tellers, so being in the smaller set automatically puts her in the larger one. The error is picking the better-fitting story over the nested-set probability relationship, which is a representativeness effect.

q: In the hospital problem which hospital has more days with over 60 percent boys, and what does the law of large numbers say?
a: The larger hospital has about 45 births a day and the smaller about 15, and about half of babies are boys. The question is which hospital records more days when over 60 percent are boys, and the correct answer is the smaller hospital. The most common response was about the same, chosen by 56 percent, which ignores how many births are behind each day’s percentage. Smaller samples vary more, so an extreme proportion is more likely in the group of 15 births, while the larger hospital’s daily proportion is more stable. Choosing the larger hospital confuses the absolute number of boys with how often an extreme proportion occurs. The law of large numbers says that as more individuals are randomly drawn, the group becomes more representative of the population. People often expect small samples to be representative too, which understates how much a small sample can vary.

q: What is an illusory correlation, and how does it connect to stereotypes and availability?
a: An illusory correlation is a relationship that appears to exist even though it does not exist or is much weaker than assumed. Stereotypes are oversimplified generalizations about a group, often emphasizing negative characteristics, and they direct attention to behaviors that fit the expected description. Selective attention and remembering the matching instances make the stereotype feel supported, so the apparent evidence is shaped by what was noticed and retained. The link to availability is that stereotype-consistent behaviors are easier to bring to mind because they got particular attention, and their availability is then mistaken for evidence that the behavior is strongly associated with the group.

q: What is myside bias and confirmation bias? What did Lord and colleagues (1979) find, and how does the 2, 4, 6 task show confirmation bias?
a: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek information that fits a hypothesis and overlook information that argues against it, and myside bias is one form of it, generating and evaluating evidence and testing hypotheses in ways biased toward one’s own opinions and attitudes. Lord and colleagues (1979) had people who favored capital punishment and people who opposed it read the same article. Those in favor interpreted it as favorable to their position and those against interpreted it as favorable to theirs, focusing on agreeing information and disregarding the rest. In the 2, 4, 6 task, participants get 2, 4, 6 as an example of a hidden rule, write their own sets of three numbers, get feedback only on whether each fits the rule, and then propose the rule. The most common hypothesis is increasing intervals of two, and testing only sequences that fit it gives repeated yes feedback. But the actual rule is any three numbers in increasing order, so only trying to disconfirm, testing the boundaries, would reveal the narrow belief is wrong.
note: In the original study participants read two mixed-evidence studies on capital punishment, not the same article, and the result is usually described as biased assimilation and attitude polarization.

q: What is expected utility theory, and why does it not fully describe what people choose?
a: Utility refers to how desirable an outcome is because it serves the person’s interests. Expected utility theory assumes people are rational and, with all relevant information, choose the alternative with maximum expected utility, combining the value of possible outcomes with their chances, and the monetary version uses the maximum expected monetary payoff. It gives specific procedures for determining the best choice. But people find value in things other than money, and many decisions do not maximize the probability of the best outcome, so people are not utility-maximization machines. Casino gambling is an example, because people choose it despite knowing the odds are strongly against them.
note: Casino gambling shows that people do not maximize expected money. It does not by itself refute expected utility theory, because utility can include enjoyment of gambling.

q: What happens in the jellybean problem, and what does it show?
a: Participants earn one dollar whenever they draw a red jellybean, up to seven dollars, and choose between two bowls. One bowl has 1 red bean out of 10, a 10 percent chance, and the other has 7 red beans out of 100, a 7 percent chance. Most participants choose the 7-out-of-100 bowl. The larger number of red beans is attractive even though the probability of drawing one is worse. A larger number of favorable items draws attention away from the denominator, the total number of possible draws, so the decision depends on considerations other than the actual probabilities of winning.
note: The slide says most participants choose the 7-out-of-100 bowl. I could not verify that a majority chose it in the original finding.

q: What happened to travel after September 11, and what does it show about risk decisions?
a: After September 11, air travel decreased and driving increased. The probability of dying in a car accident is much greater than while flying, and the reported number of Americans who died on the road while avoiding flying exceeded the total number of passengers killed on the four hijacked flights. Avoiding the feared event increased exposure to a more likely danger, because the emotional impact of the attacks is a different basis for a decision than the relative probabilities.

q: What is the convoy dilemma, and what did Ritov and Baron (1999) find?
a: A convoy of food trucks is traveling to a refugee camp during a famine, and rerouting saves 1,000 people at a second camp but 100 people in the first camp die. Rerouting has the better net count, 1,000 − 100 = 900 versus 100 − 1,000 = −900. Ritov and Baron (1999) found that 63 percent did not choose to reroute, and some would keep the original route even if only one person at the first camp would die. Reluctance to cause a loss can outweigh the larger number saved elsewhere.

q: What is the Sacred Value Protection Model (Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green and Lerner, 2000), and what are taboo and tragic tradeoffs?
a: The Sacred Value Protection Model of Tetlock, Kristel, Elson, Green and Lerner (2000) proposes that people want to protect what they hold sacred, and that sacred values are compartmentalized separately from secular values. A taboo tradeoff intermingles the sacred and secular domains, so treating a sacred concern as exchangeable for a secular benefit feels threatening and provokes moral outrage. A tragic tradeoff compares two sacred values with each other, and people are less morally outraged by it. In the taboo scenario, Robert can save Johnny, a five-year-old needing a liver transplant that costs the hospital one million dollars, or spend the money on equipment and salaries to recruit talented doctors. In the tragic scenario, two children need a liver but only one is available.

q: What did Tetlock and colleagues (2000) find about moral outrage in the Johnny scenarios?
a: In Tetlock and colleagues (2000), moral outrage was rated for taboo and tragic tradeoffs, with separate outcomes for saving Johnny and not saving him. Under the taboo tradeoff, not saving Johnny produced much greater outrage than saving him, and choosing other uses for the money instead of the child’s life received the strongest negative response. Under the tragic tradeoff, outrage was similar whether Johnny was saved or not, because choosing either child leaves another sacred concern unmet. So there is an interaction between the type of value conflict and the decision made within it.

q: What did Ginges, Atran, Medin and Shikaki (2007) study, and how did money and symbolic offers affect moral absolutists and non-absolutists?
a: Ginges, Atran, Medin and Shikaki (2007) studied sacred-value tradeoffs in an ongoing political conflict, with 601 Israeli settlers, 535 Palestinian refugees and 719 Palestinian students. They offered three deals. The taboo deal asked Palestinians to recognize the sacred and historic right of the Jewish people to Israel, with two states and a Palestinian state in 99 percent of the West Bank and Gaza. Taboo+ added a material incentive, one billion dollars a year for ten years paid by Israel. The symbolic version added Israeli recognition of the historic and legitimate right of Palestinians to their own state and an apology for wrongs done. Moral absolutists treat the issue as a sacred value and reject compromise regardless of benefit, about 46 percent of settlers for never giving up part of the Land of Israel and about 54 percent of the students for the right of return and Jerusalem. Non-absolutists also have strong preferences against compromise but do not treat the issues as sacred. For absolutists, adding money increased anger, disgust and support for violence, while for non-absolutists it reduced them. Symbolic recognition was associated with lower anger or disgust and lower support for violence, so material benefit and symbolic reciprocity are different.

q: What did Dehghani and colleagues (2009, 2010) study, and how were sacred values measured?
a: Dehghani, Atran and colleagues (2010) and Dehghani, Iliev and colleagues (2009) studied sacred values in relation to Iran’s nuclear program, asking whether people who hold the program sacred would accept material benefits or costs in exchange for compromise. An incentive offers a benefit for agreement, and a sanction is a disincentive that imposes a cost for refusing. The online study had 1,997 Iranian participants, in Farsi, and measured approval, anger, and whether a proposal seemed misleading. Using a measure based on Baron and Spranca (1997), the sacred-value response is that giving up the program should not be done no matter how great the consequences, and about 14 percent for nuclear energy and 13 percent for nuclear weapons chose it.

q: What were the deals in the study by Dehghani and colleagues (2009, 2010), and what happened for participants with a sacred value?
a: In the study by Dehghani, Atran and colleagues (2010) and Dehghani, Iliev and colleagues (2009), the design was 2 × 3, energy or weapons crossed with three deals. Taboo had Iran give up the program and its facilities to the United Nations in return for Israel doing the same, Taboo+ added 40 billion dollars from the United Nations to Iran, and Taboo− added the threat of additional sanctions if Iran refused. Participants rated their own approval, whether people would be angry if the government approved, and whether the deal seemed misleading. For energy, participants with a sacred value showed lower approval with the financial incentive and with sanctions than with the baseline, and anticipated anger was highest with the incentive and elevated with sanctions. Participants without a sacred value had much higher approval and lower anger, with little variation across conditions. So for a sacred commitment, improving the material balance does not necessarily improve acceptability.
